---
subtitle: "How AI coding assistants may and may not be used in NCC work"
---

# AI tools {#sec-ai-tools}

AI coding assistants are useful for writing and reviewing analysis code,
drafting documentation, and explaining unfamiliar code. They are also a route
by which sensitive data can leave a protected environment, because everything
typed into a hosted assistant is sent to whoever runs it.

The study group's position therefore depends on **where the assistant runs**:

- **Off-site assistants** — Claude, and UiOGPT as a secondary option — run
  outside TSD. They are used to develop analyses against a synthetic dummy
  dataset, **never against real study data**.
- **TSDGPT** runs inside TSD and is completely closed off: everything stays on
  the TSD server. It **may be used with real study data**, inside TSD.

This page explains what that means in practice.

::: {.callout-note}

## Who and what this applies to

This guidance applies to everyone doing NCC work — analysts, students,
collaborators — and to any AI assistant, whether it is a chat interface, an
editor plugin, or a command-line agent. It covers assistant use for analysis
code, documentation, and manuscript text.

It does **not** change any existing rule about data handling. Where this page
and the study's approvals or data processing agreements differ, the approvals
govern.

## The tools

| Tool | Runs | Role | Real study data? |
|------|------|------|------------------|
| **Claude** | Off-site (outside TSD) | The team's main AI work tool | **Never** — dummy data only |
| **UiOGPT** | Off-site (outside TSD) | Secondary option, if you have access | **Never** — dummy data only |
| **TSDGPT** | On-site (inside TSD) | AI assistance on the real data, inside TSD | **Yes** — inside TSD only |

TSDGPT offers a browser chat interface and an API. The API means it can also
be used from command-line coding tools inside TSD, such as aider (installed as
the `aider-chat` Python package).

The line between the two groups is not how trustworthy the provider is, but
**whether the data leaves TSD**. With Claude and UiOGPT it does; with TSDGPT it
does not.

## The rule for off-site tools

::: {.callout-important}
## Claude and UiOGPT are never used on real study data

Off-site assistants are used **only** against the synthetic dummy dataset,
outside TSD. No real NCC data goes to them in any form, and they are not
involved at any point where real data is being handled.

That means none of the following:

- rows from a real dataset, however few, including "just a couple of examples";
- a printout of the first few records, or a screenshot of the data viewer;
- identifiers, dates of birth, addresses, or free-text questionnaire answers;
- real counts or results, whether or not small cells are suppressed;
- error messages or console output produced by a run against real data;
- anything TSDGPT produced from real data — its answers are inside TSD and
  stay there.

There is no exception for a small excerpt, a de-identified-looking extract, an
assistant that claims not to train on inputs, or an enterprise account. If you
are unsure whether something counts, treat it as real data and do not share it.
:::

The dummy dataset is what makes this workable rather than merely restrictive.
Because it mirrors the real schema, an assistant that can see the dummy data
can do essentially everything it could do with the real thing — write the join,
fix the recode, debug the error — without any of the risk.

## Working off-site: develop on dummy data

The off-site assistant works on one side of the TSD boundary, real data stays on
the other, and only *code* crosses.

1. **Develop outside TSD, on dummy data.** Write and debug the analysis with
   Claude (or UiOGPT) against the dummy dataset, where it can actually run the
   code and see real errors. Iterate here until it works.
2. **Verify it yourself.** Read the finished code line by line (see
   [Verification](#verification-expectations)). This is the point at which you,
   not the assistant, take responsibility for it.
3. **Carry the code into TSD by hand.** The code crosses into TSD; the off-site
   assistant does not.
4. **Run it on the real data inside TSD.** Check the output against what the
   dummy run led you to expect.

::: {.callout-warning}
## If it fails on real data, stay inside TSD

When code works on dummy data but fails or looks wrong on the real data,
**debug it inside TSD with TSDGPT**, or **reproduce the problem in the dummy
dataset** — adjust the dummy data so it exhibits the same edge case — and debug
it there with the off-site assistant.

Do not carry the real error message, the real output, or the real values back
out to Claude or UiOGPT to ask what went wrong. That is the step this policy
exists to prevent, and it is also the step that feels most reasonable in the
moment. TSDGPT exists so that you never need to.

If the dummy dataset cannot reproduce the problem, that is worth reporting —
it usually means the dummy set is missing a pattern the real data has.
:::

## Working on-site: TSDGPT

TSDGPT runs entirely within TSD, so it can be given what off-site tools never
can: real data, real output, and real error messages. Use it for work that needs
the real data in view — debugging a failure that only happens on real data,
checking a recode against the actual values, or reviewing results.

- **Chat:** use the browser interface inside TSD.
- **Coding tools:** use the API from tools such as aider, run inside TSD.

Everything else about working in TSD still applies:

- **TSDGPT output derived from real data is real data.** Its answers, code
  comments, and summaries follow the same export rules as any other TSD
  output: only disclosure-checked aggregate results leave TSD, never
  person-level data.
- **Keep data out of version control.** Coding tools such as aider commit
  changes to git automatically. Keep data files and real output outside the
  repository the tool works in, and check its commits before any code leaves
  TSD — otherwise a commit can carry real data out with the code.
- **Keep the API key out of code.** Read it from an environment variable or a
  local configuration file that is not committed. Do not write it into scripts,
  Quarto documents, or this documentation.
- **Verification still applies.** Code from TSDGPT is a draft until a human has
  read it, exactly like code from an off-site assistant (see
  [Verification](#verification-expectations)).

::: {.callout-note}

## The dummy dataset

The dummy dataset is what makes off-site AI use possible.

::: {.callout-note}
## TODO — study team: the dummy dataset is still being built

A shared synthetic dataset mirroring the NCC schema is planned but not yet
available. Until it exists, off-site use depends on dummy data you generate
yourself (see below).

Record here, once settled:

- **where it lives** and how to get it — it is safe to distribute outside TSD,
  so it can sit alongside the analysis code;
- **what it covers** — which questionnaire families, registry variables, and
  derived variables are represented, and which are not yet;
- **who maintains it**, and how to request that a variable or a pattern be
  added;
- **how it is versioned**, so an analysis can record which version it was
  developed against;
- whether generating your own dummy data is acceptable where the shared set
  does not yet cover something.
:::

The dummy dataset mirrors the real schema — the same variable names, types, and
value labels — with entirely invented values. Two properties matter:

- **It is synthetic from scratch.** It is never sampled, perturbed, or
  reconstructed from real records. A perturbed extract of real data is still
  personal data and would defeat the whole arrangement.
- **It is safe to share freely.** Dummy data and any output derived from it can
  go to an assistant, be pasted into a conversation, or be committed alongside
  code. That is the entire point of having it.

If you generate your own dummy data because the shared set does not yet cover
what you need, follow the same rules: build it from scratch, label it
unmistakably as synthetic (a `dummy_` prefix and a header comment), and set the
study's agreed seed so it is reproducible.

```r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(936)

dummy_baseline <- tibble(
  deltaker_id = seq_len(500),
  B_Age_gr    = sample(c("18-39", "40-59", "60+"), 500, replace = TRUE),
  B_Sex       = sample(c("Female", "Male"), 500, replace = TRUE)
)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Make the dummy data hard, not tidy

Dummy data that is cleaner than the real thing produces code that breaks on
contact with the real thing. Where you know the real data has missing values,
rare categories, unexpected codes, or participants missing from a questionnaire
family, put those in the dummy set too — that is where they are cheap to
handle.
:::

## What may be shared with an off-site assistant

This table is for Claude and UiOGPT. TSDGPT, inside TSD, may also see the
right-hand column — but what it produces stays in TSD.

| Safe to share | Never share |
|---|---|
| The dummy dataset, and any output derived from it | Any real data, in any form or quantity |
| Code — R scripts, do-files, Quarto documents | Real console output, results, tables, or figures |
| Errors from a dummy-data run | Errors from a real-data run |
| Variable names, types, and factor labels (as carried by the dummy set) | Identifiers, dates of birth, addresses, free text |
| Study documentation that is already public | Credentials, internal server names, or paths |

Note what this table no longer needs to argue about. Because the dummy dataset
carries the schema and is safe by construction, questions like "may I share
variable names?" or "may I paste the codebook?" mostly answer themselves: share
the dummy set. The line is not *how sensitive is this extract* but *did it come
from real data*, which is a question you can always answer.

## Verification expectations {#verification-expectations}

::: {.callout-warning}
## AI-written code is a draft until a human has read it

An assistant produces plausible code, not verified code. This applies equally
to Claude, UiOGPT, and TSDGPT. Code that runs green against dummy data has been
shown to be *syntactically* sound and to behave sensibly on invented values —
not to be correct for the study's actual research question.
:::

Before AI-assisted code is run on real data:

1. **Read it line by line.** You are responsible for code you run on NCC data,
   whoever or whatever wrote it. If you cannot explain what a line does, do not
   run it.
2. **Check every variable name against the codebook.** A name that exists in
   the dummy set exists in the real data, but an assistant may still have
   picked the wrong variable — a plausible name from the wrong questionnaire
   family, or the wrong follow-up round.
3. **Check joins specifically.** Every NCC join is a `1:1` merge on
   `deltaker_id`; a join that changes the row count means something is wrong.
   Assert the expected row count in the code rather than checking by eye.
4. **Check the analysis answers the question you actually asked.** This is the
   failure the dummy set cannot catch: code can be flawless and still estimate
   the wrong thing.
5. **Check that disclosure control is applied.** If the code produces a table
   that will come out of TSD, confirm small-cell suppression is in the code
   before it runs, not added afterwards by hand.

::: {.callout-important}
## Dummy-data green is not real-data correct

A successful dummy run tells you the code executes. It does not tell you the
result is right. Missingness patterns, rare categories, and coding quirks in
the real data will differ from anything invented, so review real output on its
own terms rather than assuming the dummy run settled it.
:::

And for anything that reaches a manuscript:

::: {.callout-important}
No AI-generated result, table, figure, or number goes into a manuscript,
report, or presentation without a human having verified it against the analysis
output it claims to come from. The same applies to AI-drafted text making
factual claims about the study — check it against this manual.
:::

## Accounts and new tools

::: {.callout-note}
## TODO — study team: accounts, access, and new tools

The approved tools are listed under [The tools](#the-tools). Record, for each:
which account type is required (for example a team or institutional account
rather than a personal one), how to get access, and whether it may be pointed
at an analysis repository.

Record who to ask before adopting a tool that is not on the list, and note that
the question needs answering **before** first use, not after.

Off-site assistants that index a whole project directory or run commands
automatically — Claude Code is one — need particular scrutiny. On a machine
that also holds real data — an exported extract, a downloaded result, a
screenshot — such a tool can read files the user never intended to share, which
is a way real data reaches an assistant without anyone pasting anything.
:::

## If real data reaches an off-site assistant anyway

If you realise that real data of any kind has been given to Claude, UiOGPT, or
any other assistant outside TSD, treat it as a suspected personal-data breach
and report it immediately. Do not wait to establish how serious it was, and do
not try to resolve it by deleting the conversation — deletion does not undo the
transfer, and it destroys the record needed to assess what happened.

Using TSDGPT with real data inside TSD is not an incident; that is what it is
for.
